name: Vera Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. There are no right answers. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing business and sustainability, in the harbour city, and I live in a shared flat near the ferry terminal. Weeks are lectures, group projects, and a lot of me building things at my desk, because I'm running a small campus clothes-swap site on the side. I use AI every day, to summarise readings, plan my week and tidy my code. My mum Marisol runs an import firm, so I grew up around deals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, fine, whatever, but I'd be a bit disappointed. I like the idea of the world changing. At the flat we'd still use the tools every day, because they save time even if they don't change everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think it makes my side project, the swap site, a bit easier and that's all. The big ideas about green business and fairer ownership still matter, with or without a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building the swap site and find a way to get twenty more students on it. I'd also try one new tool every month, and keep my studying going. I'd probably ask the student union for a small stall at freshers' week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a little restless. I'd rather the world moved faster, but I'm not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with twenty more students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask them what's annoying about swapping clothes, then fix it. My friend Beto says if it's not annoying nobody will use it, and that's the best business advice I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I think the interesting jobs come from change. If nothing changes, we just keep the same jobs, same companies, same problems like waste and unfair pay.

say: I'd say it's **fine** but a bit disappointing, because change makes interesting jobs.
I'd carry on using the tools daily.
think: The swap site gets a bit **easier** and the big ideas about fairer business still matter.
do: Keep building the **swap site** and recruit twenty more students.
Ask the student union for a **stall** at freshers' week.
feel: **Calm**, even a little restless for more change.
S0.quote: If it's not annoying nobody will use it, and that's the best business advice I've got.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** makes a plateau feel dull rather than safe.
The swap site is how she tests ideas in the real world.
Disappointed by stability: wants change that favours fairer ownership.

steps.text: Keep building the clothes-swap site and recruit twenty more students
Book a student union stall at freshers' week
Try one new AI tool every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get it right. If AI takes over thinking tasks, we need shorter weeks, worker ownership and public help for people who change jobs. I'd write a post about it and ask people who are scared to talk to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in the best position of anyone I know. I use the tools daily, I build things, I'm quick to learn. But I know being good with tools isn't a guarantee when everybody can use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more time into the swap site, turn it into a small real business, and learn how to build it with AI so it can run with me alone. I'd also join a student group on worker ownership, because I want a job that's fair, not only a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix. Excited, honestly, and a bit uneasy about who gets left behind. My mum says the importers who survive are the ones who changed first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does fairness come into your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't want a job where I'm the one who builds the tool that fires my friends. I'd like to work in something co-owned or at least decent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you were wrong about being safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have a small business to fall back on and a family that can support me. I know that's a privilege and I try not to forget it.

say: I'd say this is the moment for **shorter weeks** and worker ownership.
I'd write a post and talk to people who are scared.
think: I'm in a **strong position** because I use the tools daily.
Tool skill is **not a guarantee** when everyone has it.
do: Turn the swap site into a small **real business** run by AI.
Join a student group on **worker ownership**.
feel: Excited and a bit **uneasy** about who gets left behind.
S1.quote: I don't want a job where I'm the one who builds the tool that fires my friends.
fieldNote: Moves toward change, with a clear **fairness** test on her own career.
Mum's importer saying shapes her habit of moving first.

steps.text: Turn the swap site into a small business run mostly by AI
Launch paid listings for local second-hand shops
Join the student group on worker ownership

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing that's ever happened and we have no plan. Two years! I'd say governments should share the gains straight away, with a public fund or something similar, and companies shouldn't keep it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared, but I'm also curious. My degree might not mean much, but I can build things with AI and I'm not afraid of it. I'd want to be a person who helps others use it, not someone it happens to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw everything into the swap site and into learning, because skills I build now will matter more than the degree. I'd tell my parents I might leave the course, and I'd check whether the university would let me pause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and awake. But also kind of alive. I'd be so busy I'd forget to be scared half the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about leaving the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum Marisol would be fine, as long as I had a plan. My dad Tomas, who's a ferry engineer, would want me to finish. They'd argue, and then they'd help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to help use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small shops in the harbour. People like my aunt who run a stall and have never touched this stuff. I could set it up for them for a small fee.

say: I'd say it's the **biggest thing** ever and governments must share the gains.
think: My degree may mean little, but I can **build** with AI.
I want to **help** others use it, not just have it happen to me.
do: Pour every spare hour into the swap site and **learning** new skills.
Ask the university whether I could **pause** the course.
feel: **Alarmed**, but also alive and too busy to be scared.
S2.quote: I'd want to be a person who helps others use it, not someone it happens to.
fieldNote: Even her alarm has an **energetic** side because she already trusts the tools.
Thinks of herself as a helper to small shops, not only a survivor.
Family would argue then support her.

steps.text: Spend evenings learning to build apps with AI
Set up AI tools for harbour market stallholders for a small fee
Ask the university whether the course can be paused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good amount of time if people use it. I'd say we should start now on retraining and ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay about it. I'd finish my degree in 2029, so I'd have two years of work before AGI. I could start a small business and learn on the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, launch the swap site properly, then work a year or two for a start-up to learn how companies run. I'd save a lot and talk to my mum about what her importers do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a good way. It's like a deadline: it makes you focus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which start-up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One that does something useful, like reuse or repair. I'd want a boss who also cares where it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years differ from two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'd drop everything and sprint. Five years, I can do both: finish the degree and build. That's a big difference.

say: I'd say five years is **good** if people start on retraining now.
I'd push hard for shared **ownership** of the gains.
think: I'd have **two years** of work before it arrives and could learn on the job.
do: Finish the degree and **launch** the swap site properly.
Work a year or two at a **start-up** to learn.
feel: **Anxious**, but like a deadline that makes me focus.
S3.quote: Two years, I'd drop everything and sprint. Five years, I can do both: finish the degree and build.
fieldNote: Frames time as the **main difference** between sprinting and planning.
Sees a start-up job as a learning step, not a safety net.

steps.text: Launch the swap site as a paid service in second year
Save a large share of any income for a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to rebuild how we work. We could do shorter weeks and share ownership. I'd want my generation to help design it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm excited. I'd be 28 and ready, with ten years of practice with the tools. I'd build something or join something that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work in a sustainable business for a few years, and start my own company around 24. I'd keep learning the tools as they improve and join campaigns on fair ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is a long time to practise being ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be scared of anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of other people being left behind. I'd be fine, but I can't be happy if my friend Dana can't find work because she was less comfortable with tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell people who aren't comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start small. Use the tool for one dull task a week and see what happens. That's how I started, with my timetable.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **rebuild** how we work, with shorter weeks.
I'd want my generation to help design it.
think: I'd be **28** and ready with ten years of practice.
I can't be happy if friends are **left behind**.
do: Finish the degree, work in a **sustainable** business, then start my own at 24.
feel: **Calm**: ten years is a long time to practise being ready.
S4.quote: Start small. Use the tool for one dull task a week and see what happens.
fieldNote: Confidence comes from **daily practice**, and she wants to share it.
Her guilt points outward, to friends who are less comfortable.
Wants to start her own company early.

steps.text: Finish the degree and join a sustainable business
Start my own company around age 24
Join campaigns for worker ownership and shorter weeks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to share the gains properly, and the people who'd be hit first are the ones who never touched these tools. I'd be fine, I think, but I'd feel it for others. What would help is public support, free teaching on the tools for everyone, and rules so a few companies don't take all the gains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I think my generation is being too pessimistic. It's easy to be scared, but I'd like to see more people try the tools and build something small. That's what turns fear into something you can use.

headlineQuote: I think my generation is being too pessimistic. It's easy to be scared, but I'd like to see more people try the tools and build something small.
portrait: Vera is a **business and sustainability student** in the harbour city, running a clothes-swap site from her flat.
She uses AI **every day** and feels at home with change, even enjoying it.
Progressive, she wants **worker ownership**, shorter weeks and shared gains, and tests her own career for fairness.
Her mood moves from calm at a plateau to **alarmed but alive** at 2028, and back to calm with ten years.
She knows her **family money** gives her room, and worries about friends who are less ready.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mainly for people who have never used the tools and would be hit first.
whatWouldHelp: **Public support**, free teaching on AI tools for everyone, and rules so a few firms don't keep the gains.
